title: The rulebook a company signs with itself
subtitle: Constitution, objects and corporate capacity
objectives: State what makes up a company's constitution under s 17, and explain the statutory-contract effect of the articles under s 33
Explain how s 31 makes a company's objects unrestricted by default, and how s 39 protects third parties from a company's lack of capacity even where the articles do restrict its objects
Apply ss 33, 39 and 171 to a new fact pattern, distinguishing a third party's protected position from a director's continuing internal duty to act within the constitution

leadingAuthorities.role: Defines what makes up a company's constitution: primarily its articles of association, together with certain qualifying resolutions and agreements
Makes a company's objects unrestricted by default, unless its articles specifically restrict them
Gives the articles the effect of a statutory contract, binding the company and each member as if under covenant
Abolishes ultra vires as against third parties: the validity of a company's act cannot be questioned on the ground of lack of capacity arising from the constitution
Retains a constitution-based limit internally, as a director's duty to act in accordance with the constitution and only exercise powers for their proper purpose

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Students often assume 'ultra vires' is dead — abolished, full stop. It's only half dead: gone as a defence available to third parties, alive and well as an internal duty directors owe the company. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You can recite the sections — this lesson checks whether you can tell which one protects an outsider and which one only binds the people inside.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below leans towards scenario questions that hinge on whether the person affected is a third party dealing with the company or a director bound by its constitution — read for that distinction first.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and take it slowly — this lesson has five statutory sections working together, and mixing up what each one actually does is the single most common source of lost marks in this topic.

overview.hook: In 1875 a House of Lords case held that a company which builds railway carriages cannot lawfully agree to finance a railway line, because building carriages — and nothing else — was what its constitution said it existed to do. The contract was void, full stop, even though everyone involved had acted in good faith. Modern company law spent well over a century dismantling that rule for anyone dealing with a company from the outside, while quietly keeping a version of it alive for the people running the company from the inside. This lesson is about both halves of that story, and about the five sections of the Companies Act 2006 that now govern it.

parts.heading: What actually makes up 'the constitution'
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part students will return to
body: Every company has a constitution, but the word covers less mystique than it sounds. Section 17 of the Companies Act 2006 defines it for the purposes of the Companies Acts: a company's constitution consists primarily of its articles of association, together with certain resolutions and agreements — chiefly special resolutions — that the Act treats as forming part of it even though they aren't physically written into the articles document itself.

The articles of association are the company's internal rulebook: they govern things like how directors are appointed and removed, how board and general meetings are run, what majorities are needed for different decisions, and how shares can be transferred. Every company must have articles; most private companies today simply adopt the relevant Model Articles prescribed under the Act, either wholesale or with bespoke amendments, rather than drafting an entire set from scratch.

It matters that the constitution is a live, alterable document, not a one-off founding charter fixed at incorporation. Companies routinely amend their articles as they grow, raise investment, or change how they're governed — and the mechanism for doing that (a special resolution, ordinarily requiring a 75% majority) is itself something s 21 of the Act regulates, sitting alongside the sections this lesson focuses on.

components.definition: A company's internal rulebook, governing matters such as directors' appointment and powers, meeting procedure, and share transfers — the core component of its constitution under s 17 of the Companies Act 2006, and (with limited exceptions) capable of amendment by special resolution.

interaction.prompt: Under s 17, is a company's constitution a fixed document that cannot be changed after incorporation?
options: No — the articles are ordinarily alterable, typically by special resolution
Yes — the constitution is fixed permanently once the company is incorporated
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. The constitution is a working document a company amends as its needs change, not a one-off founding charter frozen at incorporation.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not fixed — companies routinely alter their articles, ordinarily by special resolution, as their governance needs change over time.

parts.heading: A contract with a twist: section 33
parts.voice: statute-first — works from the text outward
body: Section 33 gives the articles legal teeth by treating them as if they were a contract — but a contract with unusual features that distinguish it sharply from an ordinary commercial agreement, and that examiners test precisely because the analogy to 'contract' is imperfect.

The section provides that the provisions of a company's constitution bind the company and its members to the same extent as if there were covenants on the part of the company and of each member to observe those provisions. In practical terms: the company can enforce the articles against a member, a member can enforce the articles against the company, and — this is the part that trips people up — a member can generally enforce the articles against another member, but only in that member's capacity as a member, not in some other capacity they might also hold, such as being a director or an outside contractor to the company.

That last limitation traces back to older case law establishing that the s 33 'contract' does not give a member (or anyone else) rights in some separate, non-membership capacity — a director who is also a shareholder cannot use s 33 to enforce a promise the articles make about how they, personally, will be treated as an employee or contractor, only rights attaching to them as a member.

components.text: The provisions of a company's constitution bind the company and its members to the same extent as if there were covenants on the part of the company and of each member to observe those provisions.
elements: Binds the company to its members
Binds each member to the company
Binds members to each other, in their capacity as members
Does not extend rights to a member in some other, non-membership capacity

interaction.prompt: Under s 33, a shareholder who is also the company's solicitor wants to enforce an article promising he will always be retained as the company's legal adviser. Can he rely on s 33 to do so?
options: No — s 33 rights attach to a person only in their capacity as a member, not in any other capacity such as solicitor or employee
Yes — s 33 protects any promise made in the articles, regardless of the capacity in which the person benefits
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct. This is the classic 'outsider rights' limitation on the s 33 statutory contract — a promise about a non-membership role is not enforceable under s 33, however clearly it's written into the articles.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at whose rights s 33 protects. It binds the company and its members qua members — a promise about someone's separate role as solicitor, director-as-employee, or outside contractor falls outside that statutory contract.

parts.heading: From 'ultra vires is fatal' to 'objects are unrestricted'
parts.voice: case-narrative — tells the story before naming the doctrine
body: To see why s 31 matters, it helps to see what it replaced. Under nineteenth-century company law, a company's memorandum of association had to state its 'objects' — the purposes it was formed to pursue — and any act outside those stated objects was ultra vires: beyond the company's legal power, and void, not merely voidable. In Ashbury Railway Carriage and Iron Co v Riche, the House of Lords held that a company formed to manufacture railway carriages had no capacity to finance the construction of a railway line, even though every director and shareholder had agreed to it: the objects clause simply didn't stretch that far, and no amount of consent inside the company could fix a contract that was void for want of capacity.

This produced real harm to innocent third parties, who could deal with a company in complete good faith, be paid, perform their side of a contract entirely — and then discover the whole arrangement was void because it fell outside the small print of an objects clause they had never read and had no realistic way to check. Companies responded by drafting ever longer, ever vaguer objects clauses to minimise the risk, which solved almost nothing and made the underlying documents nearly unreadable.

The Companies Act 2006 took a different route entirely. Section 31(1) provides that unless a company's articles specifically restrict its objects, its objects are unrestricted. For the overwhelming majority of companies today, which no longer bother including a restrictive objects clause at all, this means the ultra vires problem simply doesn't arise on the objects side — the company can lawfully do anything a natural person could do, within the ordinary bounds of the law.

components.text: Unless a company's articles specifically restrict the objects of the company, its objects are unrestricted.
elements: Restriction only where the articles specifically impose one
Most companies today choose not to restrict their objects at all

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that shows this company's objects are unrestricted under s 31.
interaction.scenarioText: A newly incorporated technology company adopts the standard Model Articles without amendment. Its articles say nothing at all about restricting the purposes for which the company may act. Its directors later decide to expand into an entirely unrelated line of business, property investment.
tappableSpans: adopts the standard Model Articles without amendment
articles say nothing at all about restricting the purposes
directors later decide to expand into an entirely unrelated line of business
interaction.correctSpan: articles say nothing at all about restricting the purposes
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Silence on objects is exactly what triggers s 31's default: no specific restriction in the articles means unrestricted objects, so the pivot into property investment raises no capacity problem at all.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the fact about what the articles do or don't say. It's the absence of any specific restriction in the articles — not the choice of Model Articles or the later business decision — that triggers the s 31 default of unrestricted objects.

parts.heading: Section 39: protecting the person on the other side of the deal
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part students will return to
body: Even where a company's articles do specifically restrict its objects — increasingly rare, but not extinct — s 39 makes sure that restriction almost never harms an outside third party dealing with the company. It provides that the validity of an act done by a company cannot be called into question on the ground of lack of capacity by reason of anything in the company's constitution.

In plain terms: even if a transaction genuinely falls outside a restricted objects clause, a third party can still hold the company to it. The old Ashbury problem — a perfectly innocent counterparty losing an entire deal because of a capacity defect buried in a document they never had reason to read — is, for third parties, effectively abolished.

It is worth being precise about what s 39 does and doesn't do. It protects the validity of the company's act as against outsiders; it does not itself authorise the directors to have entered into that transaction in the first place, and it does not stop the company (through its shareholders, or through a claim against the directors) from holding the directors to account internally for exceeding a restriction the articles genuinely imposed. That internal accountability is exactly where s 171 comes in — the subject of the final part of this lesson.

components.text: The validity of an act done by a company shall not be called into question on the ground of lack of capacity by reason of anything in the company's constitution.
elements: Protects the validity of the company's act
Operates regardless of any restriction in the constitution
Protects third parties dealing with the company, not the directors who exceeded a restriction

components.label: Section 39 at a glance
points: Even a genuinely ultra vires transaction (one outside a restricted objects clause) is valid and enforceable as against a third party
The third party does not need to prove good faith or lack of knowledge of any restriction — s 39 is not conditional on the outsider's state of mind
The protection runs to the outside party, not to the directors who caused the company to act beyond a restriction — their own accountability is a separate, internal question

interaction.prompt: In which scenario does s 39 most clearly protect the third party's position?
interaction.scenarioA: A company's articles specifically restrict it to running a bookshop. Its director, without board authority, signs a large loan agreement with a bank to fund an unrelated property purchase. The bank, unaware of the restriction, wants to enforce the loan against the company.
interaction.scenarioB: A shareholder objects internally that the same director exceeded the bookshop restriction, and wants the company to pursue the director for breach of duty over the unauthorised transaction.
interaction.explanation: A is the s 39 scenario: the bank, as an outside third party, can enforce the loan regardless of the restriction in the articles — capacity cannot be raised against it. B is a different, internal question about the director's own accountability to the company, governed by s 171 rather than s 39.

parts.heading: Ultra vires didn't die — it moved inside the company
parts.voice: reflective — closes the lesson by justifying its own place in the syllabus
body: It's tempting to treat s 39 as the end of the ultra vires story, but that misses half of what the 2006 Act actually did. Parliament abolished capacity as a defect a third party could be harmed by — but it deliberately preserved a version of the same idea as an internal constraint on directors, in s 171.

Section 171 requires a director to act in accordance with the company's constitution, and to only exercise powers for the purposes for which they are conferred. Read the first limb carefully: it is, in substance, the old ultra vires idea reborn as a directors' duty rather than a capacity rule. A director who causes the company to act outside a restriction the articles genuinely impose (rare, given s 31's default) — or who exercises a power the constitution confers for one purpose in order to achieve a quite different one (the 'proper purpose' limb, tested more fully in this module's later lessons on directors' duties) — breaches s 171, even though the transaction itself remains perfectly valid against the outside world under s 39.

This is the distinction the whole lesson has been building towards, and it is the one exam answers most often blur: s 39 asks whether the transaction is valid as against a third party (almost always yes); s 171 asks whether the director who caused the company to enter it acted properly as against the company itself (a genuinely separate question, with genuinely separate consequences — remedies for breach of duty, not the unwinding of the third party's deal). Keep the two questions apart, and this topic stops being confusing.

components.definition: A director's statutory duty to act in accordance with the company's constitution and to exercise powers only for the purposes for which they were conferred — the internal survival of the old ultra vires idea, owed to the company rather than affecting a third party's rights under a transaction. Explored fully in this module's later lessons on directors' general duties.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that s 39 makes a director's breach of a constitutional restriction entirely consequence-free?
sliderLabels: Confident — no consequences once s 39 validates the transaction
Not confident — the director can still be in breach of s 171 internally, even though the transaction is valid under s 39
interaction.correctPosition: Not confident — the director can still be in breach of s 171 internally, even though the transaction is valid under s 39
interaction.explanation: Not confident is correct. Section 39 protects the transaction's validity as against outsiders; it says nothing about the director's own position. A director who acted outside the constitution can still be pursued by the company for breach of s 171, even where the underlying deal with the third party stands.

testPool.prompt: What does s 17 of the Companies Act 2006 say makes up a company's constitution?
acceptableAnswers: the articles of association, plus certain resolutions and agreements
the articles and qualifying special resolutions
testPool.modelAnswer: Primarily the company's articles of association, together with certain resolutions and agreements — chiefly special resolutions — that the Act treats as forming part of the constitution.

testPool.prompt: Under s 31, are a company's objects restricted by default?
options: No — objects are unrestricted unless the articles specifically restrict them
Yes — every company's objects are restricted unless it opts out

testPool.prompt: Which of the following statements about s 39 is correct?
options: It protects a third party's right to enforce a transaction against the company, regardless of any capacity restriction in the constitution
It abolishes the ultra vires doctrine entirely, including as an internal directors' duty
It requires the third party to prove they acted in good faith before the transaction is protected
testPool.trapExplanation: The tempting wrong answers both overstate s 39. It does not abolish ultra vires-type reasoning internally — that survives as s 171 — and it is not conditional on the third party's good faith or state of knowledge; the protection is unconditional as to capacity.

testPool.prompt: Order these developments in the law on corporate objects and capacity.
items: Ashbury Railway Carriage and Iron Co v Riche holds a company has no capacity to act outside its stated objects
Companies routinely draft long, vague objects clauses to minimise ultra vires risk
The Companies Act 2006 makes objects unrestricted by default under s 31
Section 39 protects third parties even where a restricted objects clause is exceeded

testPool.prompt: Under s 33(1), which of the following can a member enforce against the company under the articles?
options: Rights the member holds in their capacity as a member
Rights the member holds in a separate capacity, such as employee or outside supplier
Both, without distinction

testPool.prompt: In the extract below, highlight the phrase that identifies the internal survival of the ultra vires idea after the Companies Act 2006.
testPool.passage: A director of a company must act in accordance with the company's constitution, and only exercise powers for the purposes for which they are conferred. This duty is owed to the company, and its breach does not affect the validity of the company's dealings with third parties, which section 39 separately protects.
testPool.ratioSentence: A director of a company must act in accordance with the company's constitution, and only exercise powers for the purposes for which they are conferred.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that makes s 39, rather than s 33, the relevant provision in this scenario.
testPool.scenarioText: A haulage company's articles specifically restrict it to freight transport. Its managing director, without proper authority, signs a five-year office lease on the company's behalf. The landlord, a total stranger to the company's internal affairs, wants to enforce the lease.
tappableSpans: articles specifically restrict it to freight transport
signs a five-year office lease on the company's behalf
The landlord, a total stranger to the company's internal affairs
testPool.correctSpan: The landlord, a total stranger to the company's internal affairs
testPool.explanation: The landlord is a third party seeking to enforce a transaction against the company — precisely the situation s 39 governs. Section 33 concerns rights between the company and its own members under the articles, which is not what's at stake here.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario turns on s 171 rather than s 39?
testPool.scenarioA: A supplier who dealt with the company in good faith wants to enforce a contract that, unknown to the supplier, fell outside a restriction in the company's articles.
testPool.scenarioB: The company itself wants to hold its director to account for causing it to enter that same contract, arguing the director knowingly exceeded the constitutional restriction.
testPool.explanation: B is the s 171 question: it concerns the director's internal duty to the company to act within the constitution. A is the s 39 question: the outside supplier's right to enforce the transaction, which is unaffected by any capacity restriction regardless of the director's conduct.

testPool.prompt: A charity's trading subsidiary has articles specifically restricting its objects to selling merchandise related to the charity's cause. Its sole director, acting alone, enters a large unrelated property development contract with a developer who has read the articles and knows about the restriction. The developer wants to enforce the contract. Applying s 39, does the developer succeed?
options: Yes — s 39 protects the validity of the company's act regardless of the constitutional restriction, and it does not require the third party to be unaware of that restriction
No — because the developer knew about the restriction, s 39 does not apply
No — s 39 only protects transactions that fall within the company's actual objects
testPool.explanation: Section 39 is not conditional on the third party's knowledge of any restriction. Even a developer who knew the articles restricted the company's objects can still enforce the transaction — the protection runs to the transaction's validity, unconditionally, not to innocent third parties specifically.

testPool.prompt: Does most modern practice involve companies including a restrictive objects clause in their articles?
options: No — most companies today choose unrestricted objects under the s 31 default
Yes — restrictive objects clauses remain the standard, default drafting choice

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that s 39 and s 171 protect the same interest?
sliderLabels: Confident — they protect the same thing
Not confident — s 39 protects third parties' transactions, s 171 protects the company against its own directors
testPool.correctPosition: Not confident — s 39 protects third parties' transactions, s 171 protects the company against its own directors
testPool.explanation: Correct to be unconfident they're the same. Section 39 is an external protection running to third parties dealing with the company; s 171 is an internal duty a director owes to the company itself. A single set of facts can trigger one, the other, or both, but they answer different questions.

testPool.prompt: A private company's articles specifically restrict its objects to operating a single named restaurant. Without consulting the board, one director signs a contract on the company's behalf to open a second, unrelated nightclub venue with an outside investor who has not read the articles. The investor later wants to enforce the contract, and separately the company's shareholders want to know whether they have any claim against the director. Analyse both questions.
factsToOrder: The articles specifically restrict the company's objects to the named restaurant
The director signs a contract for an unrelated nightclub venue without board approval
The outside investor has not read the articles and is unaware of the restriction
The investor wants to enforce the contract
The shareholders ask whether they have a claim against the director

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the investor can enforce the nightclub contract despite the constitutional restriction, and separately whether the shareholders have any claim against the director for entering it.
modelAnswer.rule: Section 39 protects the validity of a company's act against a third party regardless of any capacity restriction in the constitution, and does not require the third party's good faith. Section 171 separately requires a director to act in accordance with the constitution and only exercise powers for their proper purpose, a duty owed to the company.
modelAnswer.application: The investor's position is governed by s 39: even though the contract falls outside the restricted objects, its validity cannot be questioned on that ground, and the investor's lack of awareness of the restriction is irrelevant either way — the contract stands. The director's position is governed by s 171: by causing the company to act outside the constitution without board approval, the director has likely breached the duty to act within the company's constitution, exposing them to a claim by the company (and, depending on the circumstances, action by the shareholders) for breach of duty.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The investor can enforce the contract under s 39. Separately, and without affecting that enforceability, the shareholders likely do have a claim against the director for breach of the s 171 duty to act within the company's constitution.

testPool.prompt: A student writes: 'Since s 39 abolishes ultra vires, directors can never be held to account for exceeding what the company's constitution allows.' What is wrong with this statement?
options: It correctly summarises the effect of s 39
It conflates the abolition of ultra vires as against third parties with the survival of a constitution-based duty owed internally by directors under s 171
It confuses s 39 with s 33, which governs the statutory contract between members
testPool.trapExplanation: This is the single most common error in this topic. Section 39 only removes capacity as a defect affecting third parties; it says nothing about directors' internal accountability, which s 171 preserves in substance. Treating 'ultra vires is abolished' as a blanket statement misses that half of the old doctrine survives, just relocated.

testPool.prompt: Name the five sections of the Companies Act 2006 covered in this lesson and, in a phrase, what each governs.
acceptableAnswers: s 17 constitution, s 31 objects, s 33 statutory contract, s 39 third-party capacity, s 171 director's duty to act within powers
testPool.modelAnswer: Section 17 (what the constitution comprises), s 31 (objects unrestricted by default), s 33 (the articles as a statutory contract), s 39 (protecting third parties from lack-of-capacity arguments), and s 171 (a director's duty to act within the constitution and for proper purposes).

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is treating s 39's abolition of ultra vires as total — forgetting that the same idea survives internally as a director's duty under s 171. Whenever a fact pattern involves both an outside party and the company's own directors, expect the question to test whether you can separate the third party's protected position from the director's continuing internal accountability.
